short: A three-tiered stone bridge carried the Nîmes aqueduct across the Gardon at barely a hair's fall.
full:
The Pont du Gard, in what is now southern France, carried the aqueduct supplying the Roman colony of Nemausus (Nîmes) across the Gardon river gorge. Long attributed to Agrippa around 19 BCE, archaeological evidence, including coins no older than Claudius's reign found at the outlet, now dates its construction to roughly 40–60 CE. An estimated 800 to 1,000 workers built the three tiers of arches, the highest reaching 49 metres, without mortar in the visible facing, the stone blocks held by friction and iron clamps.

The aqueduct ran some 50 kilometres from a spring near Uzès to Nîmes, dropping only about 17 metres over that distance, a gradient of extraordinary precision for surveying tools of the period. It supplied the city's baths, fountains and private houses for roughly five centuries before neglect and stone-robbing reduced its flow. The bridge itself survived intact, reused as a toll crossing through the Middle Ages and later restored, and remains one of the best-preserved works of Roman civil engineering.
